issues.legal_issue: A liquidator may disclaim leased land only when the court is fully satisfied that its covenants impose a heavy burden on the company in liquidation.
material_facts: The company held land under a 99-year lease, renewable for a further 99 years, at a rent of Rs 1,200 per annum.
The lessor’s successor sought disclaimer, alleging that rent arrears and possible liability for mesne profits made the lease onerous.
The bank opposed disclaimer, said the leasehold was valuable security, and offered to pay the rent arrears.
The land and the mill standing on it were ultimately sold together as a going concern, free of the leasehold rights.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in permitting disclaimer: the power under Section 535 of the Companies Act, 1956, must be exercised cautiously, and the lease was not shown to impose a heavy burden on the company.
issues.legal_principle: Section 535 of the Companies Act, 1956 empowers the High Court to permit a liquidator to disclaim land burdened with onerous covenants. The provision protects the company’s creditors from onerous obligations, but disclaimer seriously disadvantages the beneficiary of the covenants, so the court must exercise due care and be fully satisfied that the covenants impose a heavy burden. The court considered it unjustified, in disclaimer proceedings, to determine that the lease had been validly terminated and to treat resulting mesne profits and rent arrears as making the lease onerous. No earlier cases are relied upon.

rule.if: disclaimer_application_in_liquidation and long_term_low_rent_lease and not substantial_burden_shown

predicates.disclaimer_application_in_liquidation: A party sought permission for a liquidator to disclaim property of a company in liquidation.
predicates.long_term_low_rent_lease: The company held the land under a long-term lease at a low rent.
predicates.substantial_burden_shown: The evidence established that the lease covenants imposed a heavy burden on the company in liquidation.

issues.definition: When a disclaimer application concerns a company’s long-term, low-rent lease and no heavy burden is established, disclaimer is not justified.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for a lessor’s rights in land sold with a company’s assets must account for the value of those rights and may be fixed by the court as a full settlement of related claims.
material_facts: The land was subject to a long lease with a renewal option and a low annual rent, factors that substantially depressed the value of the lessor’s interest.
The Court directed that the land be sold free of the leasehold rights as part of the company’s assets.
The Trust had already received Rs 7.5 lakhs under an earlier court order, subject to later adjudication of its rights.

The Court assessed compensation for the Trust’s rights in the land and rent arrears, and directed payment of the unpaid balance from the company’s funds in full and final settlement of its claims concerning the land.
issues.conclusion: The Trust was entitled to total compensation of Rs 10 lakhs in full and final settlement of its claims concerning the land, with the unpaid balance payable by the Official Liquidator.
issues.legal_principle: The Court’s directions for a court-supervised sale free of leasehold rights left it to determine the amount payable from the company’s funds for the lessor’s rights. In assessing that compensation, the Court considered the duration and renewal terms of the lease, the low rent and the effect of those terms on the value of the lessor’s interest, as well as arrears of rent. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this assessment.

predicates.court_supervised_liquidation_sale: The court directed the liquidator to sell the company’s property and assets.
predicates.land_sold_free_of_leasehold_rights: The sale directed by the court included the land free of its leasehold rights.
predicates.lessor_rights_require_compensation: The lessor’s rights in the land were disposed of and required compensation.

issues.definition: When a court-supervised liquidation sale transfers land free of leasehold rights and the lessor’s rights require compensation, the court fixes compensation as a full settlement.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser at a court-supervised sale of a company’s assets cannot obtain a price reduction for defects in title, description, or possession when the sale terms place verification on the purchaser and disclaim any warranty by the liquidator.
material_facts: The sale terms provided that the assets were sold on an “as is where is” basis and that the liquidator gave no guarantee or warranty concerning them.
The sale terms required intending purchasers to satisfy themselves about title, encumbrances, area and other details, and excluded compensation or a price deduction for defects.
The purchaser alleged that it had not received possession of certain properties and that the company did not own them.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to a reduction in the sale price on account of the alleged defects or failure to hand over possession.
issues.legal_principle: When a liquidator sells company property under court orders on terms disclaiming warranties and requiring the purchaser to verify title, encumbrances and description, the purchaser cannot later claim a price reduction for defects in those matters. The Court distinguished this court-supervised sale from an individual’s sale of property belonging to that individual. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

rule.if: court_supervised_liquidation_sale and sale_terms_disclaim_warranty and purchaser_responsible_for_verification and purchaser_alleges_property_defects

predicates.court_supervised_liquidation_sale: A liquidator sold company property under the court’s orders.
predicates.sale_terms_disclaim_warranty: The sale terms stated that the liquidator gave no warranty or guarantee concerning the property.
predicates.purchaser_responsible_for_verification: The sale terms placed responsibility on the purchaser to verify the property’s title, encumbrances, description and other details.
predicates.purchaser_alleges_property_defects: The purchaser alleged defects in title, description or possession of the property.

issues.definition: A purchaser at a court-supervised liquidation sale cannot obtain a price reduction for alleged property defects when the sale terms disclaim warranties and place verification on the purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser must pay interest in accordance with an unequivocal payment undertaking accepted by the court, notwithstanding a claim for a reduction in the purchase price.
material_facts: The purchaser undertook to pay the outstanding purchase price with interest at 15 per cent per annum from the specified start date, and the Court accepted the undertaking.
The purchaser paid the outstanding principal after delay.
The purchaser also sought a reduction in the purchase price based on alleged failures to deliver possession of certain properties.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was ordered to pay interest on the outstanding principal in accordance with its undertaking, and its claim for a price reduction did not excuse that payment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court enforced the purchaser’s unequivocal undertaking, accepted by the Court, to pay interest on the outstanding purchase price. It also found interest appropriate in light of the delay in payment. The purchaser’s separate claim for a price reduction was rejected under the terms of the court-supervised sale. No statutory provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

predicates.contempt_proceeding_concerning_sale_obli: The proceeding concerned enforcement of obligations arising from a court-supervised sale.
predicates.court_accepted_interest_undertaking: The purchaser gave an unequivocal undertaking to pay interest, and the court accepted it.
predicates.purchaser_delayed_payment: The purchaser did not pay the outstanding purchase price when required and paid it later.

issues.definition: In a proceeding concerning court-supervised sale obligations, a purchaser who delayed payment must pay interest when the court accepted the purchaser’s undertaking to do so.
